A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LIHF research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing renamed and relocated material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic dueling-bandit simulations and Spotify recommendation experiments, including regret curves, fitted growth orders, and repeated-run summaries in Section 6 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic simulations, regret curves, fitted growth orders, and repeated-run summaries in Section 5 and Appendix E. Results retained from v1 still qualify.

M1.justification: RoSMID in v2 Algorithm 1 matches the perturbation, gradient estimator, and mirror-descent update of v1 Algorithm C.1. Its corruption-dependent learning-rate schedule already appears in v1 Proposition C.1. DBGD's procedure is also retained; renaming and promoting the mirror-descent method do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: v2 removes Spotify recommendation evaluation, including the 170,000-song dataset and 2,000-song subset, eliminating the real-data domain and discrete, nonconvex action-space evaluation. It retains quadratic-utility synthetic simulations but also removes the dedicated two-dimensional linear-utility experiment.

E2.justification: Versatile-DB, actually evaluated against DBGD in v1 Appendix D.2.1 and Figure D.4, disappears with that comparison. Doubler and Sparring remain in the synthetic comparisons. RoSMID corresponds to the previously evaluated NC-SMD variant, rather than an additional comparator.

E3.justification: The known-ρ parameter sweep adds ρ=0.7 in v2 Figure 1 to the values shown in v1 Figure D.1. Retained simulations preserve d=5, T=100,000, radius 10, quadratic utility, logistic link, and last-1% slope fitting. v2 Figure 2's arbitrary-corruption prose and decaying-corruption caption leave its corruption description ambiguous; they do not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 removes the constructed experiment validating DBGD's lower bound and the separately documented first-C-round arbitrary-corruption robustness comparison from v1 Figures 2 and 3. The known-ρ analysis, decaying-corruption comparison, and learning-rate sensitivity grid survive as v2 Figures 1–3. Thus distinct convergence and robustness validation questions lose their experimental evidence.

E5.justification: The retained experiments continue to report five simulations and mean plus or minus one standard deviation. The separate 50-seed DBGD lower-bound study and its individual-run traces are removed. No increase in repetitions or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported for retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 removes all Spotify outcomes, the DBGD lower-bound simulation's fitted order of 0.76, and the separate arbitrary-corruption comparison. The results in v1 Figures D.2 and D.3 are retained under renamed displays. v2 Figure 1 adds a ρ=0.7 curve with fitted order 0.47 while retaining the previously displayed known-ρ results.

T1.justification: v2 adds RoSMID's corruption-free Ω(T^α) lower bound and Lemma 22, and extends DBGD's Ω(T^(3/4)) result at α=1/4 to Ω(T^(1−α)) throughout the stated parameter range. It removes v1 Appendix A's generalized-learnability definition and supporting lemmas, and revises an Abel-summation exponent from ρ−1/2 to ρ−2. The matching known-ρ upper bound and core mirror-descent analysis already existed in v1 Appendix C.3.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds unknown arbitrary corruption, efficiency–robustness tradeoffs, and real-world recommendation validation. v2 centers near-optimal learning with known ρ and decaying corruption, presenting the analysis framework as a principal contribution and the agnostic setting as an additional application. It removes the real-data validation claim and strengthens the parameterized efficiency lower-bound claims.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies v1's categorical interpretation that imperfect feedback is no easier than arbitrary corruption: the introduction now calls this a 'hint' because the compared settings differ. It explicitly discusses unresolved tightness under arbitrary corruption and interprets the new lower bounds as unavoidable efficiency costs. Spotify-specific explanations and claims of applicability to discrete, nonconvex actions disappear.

D1.justification: v2 removes the simulation corruption recipe based on v1 Definition A.1, including λ=2, the corruption-scale constant set to 0.1 times the utility range, and the adversarial sign rule. Spotify preprocessing, clustering instructions, data-source information, and Versatile-DB's reported CPU cost also disappear. The missing corruption-generation details materially reduce reproducibility of the retained simulations.

R1.justification: v2 refocuses positioning on continuous actions with strictly concave utilities versus finite-arm and linear-utility methods, narrowing the novelty claim and emphasizing the NC-SMD generalization. It removes much of the broader stochastic-bandit survey and associated citations, adds Di et al. (2023), and changes the retained linear-bandit lower-bound attribution from Lattimore and Szepesvári (2020) to Dani et al. (2008).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem framing, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work is integrated into the introduction, the appendix mirror-descent analysis becomes a central section with a four-step proof narrative, DBGD becomes secondary, and the appendices are reorganized. These are substantial narrative changes beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 removes the tradeoff schematic, DBGD lower-bound plot, separate arbitrary-corruption plot, and both Spotify figures. Appendix plots D.1 and D.2 become main-text Figures 1 and 2, with revised titles and displays; the sensitivity grid becomes Figure 3 with an expanded caption. Mirror-descent and DBGD algorithm boxes exchange main-text and appendix placement.

improvement.justification: v2 offers a clearer account of the known-ρ analysis, more careful cross-setting qualifications, expanded efficiency lower-bound arguments, and a correction within the Abel-summation derivation. However, it narrows empirical validation and removes essential corruption-generation details, while Figure 2's prose and caption leave its setting ambiguous. The theoretical and explanatory gains coexist with material reproducibility losses, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
